stem: What are the two essential parts of every recursive function?

options.text: A loop and a condition
A base case (stopping condition) and a recursive case (calling itself with a smaller input)
A return value and a print statement
An accumulator and a counter

explanation_after: Every recursive function needs: (1) a base case that returns a value without recursing, and (2) a recursive case that breaks the problem into smaller pieces and calls itself.

stem: What error does Python raise when recursion goes too deep?

options.text: OverflowError
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
MemoryError
RuntimeError

explanation_after: Python limits recursion to ~1000 calls (configurable via sys.setrecursionlimit). Exceeding this raises RecursionError to prevent the call stack from consuming all available memory.

stem: Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponentially slow. The fix is:

options.text: Using a faster computer
Memoisation — caching results so each subproblem is computed only once
Increasing the recursion limit
Using smaller Fibonacci numbers

explanation_after: fib(n) recomputes fib(n-2) for every branch. With memoisation (@functools.cache or @lru_cache), each value is computed exactly once, reducing O(2ⁿ) to O(n).

stem: What does `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)` do on a recursive function?

options.text: Converts it to iteration
Caches return values so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly
Limits how many times it can recurse
Increases the recursion limit

explanation_after: lru_cache stores (args → result) pairs. On a subsequent call with the same args, it returns the cached result instead of recomputing. For recursive functions this avoids exponential recomputation.

stem: When is recursion MORE natural than iteration?

options.text: When processing flat lists
When the problem involves tree/graph structures or nested data of unknown depth
When performance is critical
When the input is always small

explanation_after: Recursion maps naturally onto tree-shaped problems: file systems, HTML DOMs, JSON objects, and abstract syntax trees. The recursive structure of the code mirrors the recursive structure of the data.

stem: What is the purpose of the accumulator pattern in recursion?

options.text: To count how many times the function has been called
To carry intermediate results as a parameter, avoiding the need to multiply/add on the way back up the call stack
To prevent infinite recursion
To increase performance by skipping computation

explanation_after: In `fact_tail(n, acc=1)`, instead of `n * fact(n-1)` (which needs to wait for the return), we pass the accumulated result as `acc`, making the recursive call the last operation (tail call).

stem: A decision tree is built with this idea: to build a tree for a dataset, pick the best feature to split on, then build a tree for each resulting subset. Why is this naturally a recursive algorithm?

options.text: Because trees are always slower than lists
Because building a tree for a subset is the same problem — build a tree for a dataset — applied to smaller data, with a base case of a subset that's pure enough (or empty) to stop splitting
Because decision trees require a fixed number of loops
Because Python requires recursion for any tree-shaped structure

explanation_after: Decision tree construction (e.g. CART, ID3) is a textbook example of recursion: build_tree(data) calls build_tree(subset) on each split, with a base case where a node becomes a leaf (data is pure, too small, or a max depth is reached). This recursive structure directly mirrors the tree-shaped data it produces.

stem: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each layer's weights by starting at the output layer and working backward, where each layer's gradient calculation reuses the gradient already computed for the layer after it. Which recursion concept does this resemble?

options.text: A base case with no recursive case at all
Memoisation — each layer's gradient is like a cached subproblem result, reused rather than recomputed from scratch
Infinite recursion with no termination
A recursive call with no base case, since neural networks have no natural stopping point

explanation_after: Just like memoised recursive Fibonacci reuses fib(n-1)'s cached result instead of recomputing it, backpropagation reuses the gradient already computed at layer L+1 when computing the gradient at layer L, via the chain rule. This reuse is why backprop is efficient rather than recomputing the chain rule from scratch for every single weight.
